Textual means of, relating to, found in, or based on a text.

That's the heart of it. Whenever something is described as "textual," it is being connected — in some way — to written words. It is the adjective form of the noun text.

Before going further, you need to have a clear picture of "text," because "textual" grows directly out of it.

A text is any piece of writing considered as an object of study or reference — a novel, a poem, a news article, a contract, a speech transcript, a religious scripture, an essay, an email, a law. The word "text" in this sense doesn't just mean "some writing." It means writing that you can point to, examine, quote from, or analyze. It is a body of words that exists as a stable, readable thing.

So "textual" = "having to do with that body of words."

There are two main ways "textual" is used, and understanding both will give you complete mastery of the word.

Sense 1 — Relating to the actual words of a specific text

This is the most common and important sense. Here, "textual" means drawn from, found within, or belonging to the words of a particular piece of writing.

When someone says "textual evidence," they mean evidence that comes directly from the written words of the text itself — specific lines, sentences, or passages you can point to on the page. If a teacher asks you to support your argument with textual evidence, they want you to quote or closely reference what the author actually wrote, not just share your personal opinion.

When someone says "textual analysis," they mean the close, careful examination of the actual words in a piece of writing — how sentences are constructed, what specific words are chosen, how meaning is built through the language on the page.

When someone says "textual interpretation," they mean figuring out the meaning of a piece of writing by paying close attention to what the words say and how they say it.

The key idea in this sense: textual always ties you back to the words themselves. It's an anchor to the written material.

Sense 2 — Relating to text as a form or medium

Here, "textual" describes something that exists in the form of text — as written or printed words — as opposed to some other form like images, audio, or numbers.

"Textual content" in a document means the written words, as opposed to images or charts embedded in it. "Textual data" in computing means information stored as readable characters and words, as opposed to binary data, numerical data, or image files. A novel is textual. A photograph is not. An audio recording is not. A spreadsheet full of numbers is only partially textual.

This sense is especially common in technology, linguistics, and information science.
A Crucial Distinction: Textual vs. Contextual

This is one of the most useful contrasts to understand, and it will sharpen your use of the word considerably.

Textual refers to what the words themselves say — the internal world of the writing.

Contextual refers to the surrounding circumstances, background information, or external situation — things outside the writing that help you understand it.

If you are doing a textual reading of a poem, you are sticking strictly to the words the poet wrote — the imagery, the phrasing, the structure. You are not bringing in information about the poet's life or the historical period.

If you are doing a contextual reading, you are pulling in that outside information — the author's biography, the political events of the time, the audience the work was written for — to help you interpret it.

Both approaches are valid and often used together. But "textual" specifically keeps you inside the text.

These two words are related but not the same, and confusing them is a common mistake.

Literary carries a sense of artistic quality or creative value. We call a novel "literary" to suggest it has depth, craft, and artistic merit. The word can also simply mean "relating to literature."

Textual is more neutral and analytical. It doesn't imply artistic quality. A dry legal contract is not "literary," but it absolutely has textual features — it has words, sentences, structure, and language that can be analyzed. Any piece of writing can be discussed textually.

So "textual" is the broader, more purely analytical word. "Literary" is narrower and often implies artistic writing.

These are the phrases you'll most often see "textual" appear in:

  • Textual evidence — specific written proof drawn from a text
  • Textual analysis — close examination of the words and language in a text
  • Textual interpretation — reading and assigning meaning to written words
  • Textual criticism — the scholarly practice of examining multiple versions or manuscripts of a text to determine its most accurate or original form (common in Biblical studies and classical literature)
  • Textual features — characteristics of how a piece of writing is structured, worded, or organized (e.g., headings, tone, sentence length, word choice)
  • Textual content — the written portion of a document or medium
  • Textual data — information in readable, written character form
  • Textual clues — hints or signals found in the words of a text
  • Textual support — written evidence from a text used to back up an argument or claim
  • Textual variant — a difference in wording between two different versions or copies of the same text (used in historical and biblical scholarship)
  • Textual coherence / cohesion — how well the sentences and ideas in a piece of writing hold together and flow logically
A Few Illustrative Examples in Sentences

• "The student's essay lacked textual evidence — she made claims without quoting the story."
  • "The historian performed a textual analysis of the ancient manuscript to understand its political message."
  • "The difference between the two editions of the Bible is a matter of textual variants introduced by medieval copyists."
  • "Search engines primarily index textual content; they cannot read the words embedded inside an image."
  • "Her interpretation went beyond the textual; she drew heavily on the author's biography."
  • "The legal team argued based on the textual meaning of the clause — exactly what the words said, nothing more."

If you ever need to recall what "textual" means in a flash:

Textual = of or relating to text — specifically, to the actual written words of a piece of writing, or to something that exists in written form.

Everything else — the distinctions, the collocations, the contexts — flows from that core.
